title: Lawn Mowing Pricing: How Much to Charge per Yard
description: Price mowing by time and hourly rate, not by guess. Worked yard example, per-visit and monthly math, plus a checklist to use today.

cover.alt: A lawn care worker walking to a mower on a trailer behind a pickup truck

tool.name: Lawn mowing price calculator
tool.short: Price per visit and per month

keywords: how much to charge for mowing
takeaways: HomeGuide puts most residential mowing at $30 to $85 per visit, with about $50 as a common middle price.
Price from time: minutes on site plus travel, times your target hourly rate, divided by 60.
Set a minimum charge and hold it, even for the smallest yard on your route.
body:
Charge $30 to $85 per visit for most residential yards, and build your own price from time, not from what the truck down the street charges. Time yourself on site, add travel and loading, then multiply by the hourly rate your business needs to earn. The worked example below lands on $60 per visit for a quarter acre yard, which sits right in the normal market range.

## The pricing formula

**Price per visit = (minutes on site + travel and load minutes) / 60 x your target hourly rate.**

**Monthly price = price per visit x visits per month.**

Your target hourly rate has to cover labor, fuel, blades, truck cost, insurance, taxes, and profit. If you have not set that rate yet, work it out first with our [contractor hourly rate calculator](/blog/contractor-hourly-rate-calculator/). A price that looks fine at $40 per hour can lose money once a helper, drive time, and a mower payment enter the picture.

Market data gives you a sanity check, not your price. HomeGuide lists lawn mowing at $30 to $85 per visit. A 2026 summary of HomeGuide data lists weekly service at $30 to $40 for about 1/8 acre, $45 to $65 for about 1/4 acre, $50 to $75 for about 1/2 acre, and $60 to $100 for about 1 acre. Biweekly and monthly visits cost more per visit because the grass is taller and the work is slower.

| Lawn size | Weekly, per visit | Biweekly, per visit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| About 1/8 acre | $30 to $40 | $40 to $50 |
| About 1/4 acre | $45 to $65 | $60 to $85 |
| About 1/2 acre | $50 to $75 | $65 to $100 |
| About 1 acre | $60 to $100 | $80 to $150 |

Use the table after you run your own math. If your number is far below the table, you are probably forgetting travel, trimming, or cleanup time. If it is far above, check whether the yard has a slope, a tight gate, or heavy trimming that really does cost more.

## Worked example: a quarter acre yard, weekly

A client has a flat quarter acre lot, about 10,890 sq ft (1,012 sq m) of lot, with a normal fence line, two small trees, and a driveway to edge. You time a test cut.

Step 1: Mow time is 25 minutes. Trim and edge time is 10 minutes. Blow-off time is 5 minutes. Total on site = 40 minutes.

Step 2: Travel from the last job, plus load and unload, is 20 minutes. Total paid time = 40 + 20 = 60 minutes.

Step 3: Your target rate is $60 per hour for a solo operator. Price = 60 / 60 x $60 = $60 per visit.

Step 4: Weekly service in a 4-visit month = $60 x 4 = $240 per month. In a month with 5 cuts, quote the per-visit price or set a monthly price based on 4.33 average weeks. $60 x 4.33 = $259.80, so a flat $260 monthly price is fair and easy to explain.

Check the math a second way. On-site work alone is 40 minutes, or two thirds of an hour. Two thirds x $60 = $40. Travel is one third of an hour, or $20. $40 + $20 = $60 per visit. Both methods agree.

Check it against the market. $60 sits inside the $45 to $65 weekly range for a quarter acre in the table above. You can quote it with confidence and show the client it covers mow, trim, edge, and blow-off.

## What moves a yard up or down in price

Grass height moves price the most. A first cut on an overgrown yard can take twice as long as a weekly cut. Quote first cuts as a separate cleanup price, often 1.5 to 2 times the normal visit price, then start the regular rate on the next visit.

Access matters. A 36 in gate that forces a push mower on a large back yard adds real minutes. So do steep slopes, ditches, trampolines, dog waste, hoses, and toys left in the grass. Walk the yard before you quote, and note every item you will have to move or trim around.

Route density matters too. Five yards on one street share one drive. A lone yard 15 minutes away carries the full travel cost on its own. Price lone yards at your full time cost, and give your best prices to tight routes that fill a day.

Frequency changes the per-visit price. Weekly yards are fast and clean. Biweekly yards in peak growth can need double passes. Price biweekly at 10 to 30 percent more per visit, and say so up front. Our [markup vs margin calculator](/blog/markup-vs-margin-calculator/) helps if you price add-on work like aeration or cleanup by cost plus markup.

## A checklist you can use today

Use this list on every new quote, in this order.

- Measure or pace the lot and note the grass area, not just the lot size.
- Time a full cut once, or estimate mow, trim, edge, and blow minutes in writing.
- Add travel and load minutes from your last stop, not from your shop.
- Multiply total minutes by your hourly rate and divide by 60.
- Compare the result with the market table and adjust only for real yard factors.
- State the minimum charge, the visit price, and what is included, in one line.
- State the overgrowth rule and the biweekly price before the first cut.
- Put the quote in writing with our [free estimate template](/blog/free-estimate-template/).

Extras need their own lines. Spring cleanup, leaf removal, hedge work, and fertilizer are not part of a mow price unless you list them. HomeGuide lists lawn fertilizing at $65 to $100 per application and yard cleanup at $125 to $400, which shows why folding extras into a mow price cuts your pay fast. Price hand work with the same time method you use in our [handyman pricing calculator](/blog/handyman-pricing-calculator/) if you take small repair jobs between routes.

## Common pricing mistakes

The first mistake is pricing by lot size alone. Two quarter acre yards can differ by 20 minutes of trimming. Time is the cost, so time is the price base.

The second mistake is no minimum. A tiny yard still needs a drive, an unload, and a load-up. Set a floor, for many solo operators $35 to $45, and hold it kindly and firmly.

The third mistake is chasing a low competitor. You do not know his costs, his tax setup, or how long he will last. Match on route fit and reliability, not on his lowest yard.

The fourth mistake is silent scope creep. If a client asks for branch pickup or bed weeding at every visit, add a line price that week. Small free extras, repeated 30 times a season, are a real pay cut.

## Frequently asked questions

### How much should I charge to mow a quarter acre?
Most weekly quarter acre yards price at $45 to $65 per visit in 2026 market data. Run your time math first. A 60-minute total job at a $60 hourly rate is $60 per visit, or about $240 to $260 per month on weekly service.

### Should I charge by the hour or by the yard?
Quote by the yard, price by the hour. Clients want one flat visit price. You should build that price from your timed minutes and your hourly rate, then keep timing your yards as you get faster or add a helper.

### How much extra for biweekly mowing?
Add 10 to 30 percent per visit over your weekly price. Taller grass slows the mower and the trimmer, and clippings take longer to clean up. State the biweekly price in the first quote, not after the first heavy cut.

### What minimum charge should a solo mower set?
Set a minimum that covers a short drive, load and unload, and at least 20 minutes on site. For many solo operators that lands at $35 to $45. If a yard cannot meet your minimum, it needs to sit next to another yard on the same stop.

### How do I price an overgrown first cut?
Walk it, then price it as a cleanup at 1.5 to 2 times the normal visit price, or by timed hours at your full rate. Take photos before you start. Once the yard is at normal height, move it to the regular visit price.
